structure.title: Do people bunch at the income-based fine cutoffs?
Does a larger speeding ticket influence re-offending? (specification, validity, results, heterogeneity, robustness)
What explains the smooth distributions and reactions to a larger fine?
Distributional implications of income-based versus fixed fines

observations.statement: The reoffending analysis is framed as a sharp regression discontinuity design; the coefficient on the cutoff indicator is named the specific deterrence effect of larger fines on cumulative recidivism at each monthly horizon.
observations.quote: using a sharp regression discontinuity design (RDD)

observations.statement: The identifying assumption is stated as smoothness of potential outcomes at the cutoff, with the interpretation that individuals at the cutoff are similar on average but receive very different fine sizes.

A named threat is that fixed and income-based fines could differ in license-suspension risk or in future fine sizes; the author argues from institutional rules that both accumulate points identically, and adds a footnote on prior-year ticket prevalence.

Crossing the cutoff is later used as an instrument for the euro fine amount; three IV assumptions (relevance, independence, exclusion) are listed and each is tied to a figure or institutional argument.
The bunching section states the theoretical prediction (excess mass below the notch) and tests it visually with density plots in two data sources rather than with a formal bunching estimator.

The author explicitly discusses that the absence of bunching in camera data could reflect drivers slowing before known cameras, and uses the anonymous full-traffic distributions and one co-located station to address it.

Primary data are police speeding tickets over a stated two-year window, linked via personal identifiers to the crime report register, the FOLK population module, accident data and an anonymous traffic monitoring dataset; each source is cited as a data reference.

Sample restrictions are listed in a dedicated subsection: camera-measured tickets only (officer discretion cited as the reason), dropping the highest speed limit zone for sparse data, requiring personal identifiers and adult age.
A further exclusion of one speed limit zone from the main RD analysis is justified by an unexplained mass point suspected to be a data error, with an appendix figure showing results using all zones.
The end of the sample period is explained by a reform after which fixed fines are no longer observed.
The author states that the same individuals can be followed for a fixed number of months, after which the follow-up sample shrinks, and refers to the robustness section for this limitation.
Observation counts are reported per column in the descriptives table, per row (horizon) in the main RD table together with the selected bandwidth, and per column in the IV table.
The unit is a speeding ticket event indexed by individual and speed limit zone, with time normalized to the ticket date.

The main outcome is a cumulative indicator for any new traffic crime within t months after the ticket, built monthly from crime report data; non-traffic crime and accident-as-driver indicators are built analogously.

The running variable is police-adjusted speed measured as distance from the income-based fine cutoff, pooled across speed limit zones by normalization; all speeds reported are the police-adjusted ones.
Treatment is crossing the income-based cutoff; the treatment contrast is shown as the average fine jump in a figure, with an appendix figure showing how it varies with income.

Monthly income at the time of the ticket is proxied by annual net income; the author flags modest measurement error and shows in an appendix figure that the proxy correlates with income backed out from the fine.
A covariate summary index is built by regressing reoffending on predetermined covariates in the fixed-fine group only and predicting for everyone; it is used as a single balance outcome.
Income quartiles for heterogeneity are defined from predetermined income measured one to two years before the ticket; the exact lag is stated in figure and table notes.

The main RD table has one row per monthly horizon and columns for control mean, baseline estimate, estimate with controls, bias-corrected CCT estimate, bandwidth and observations; checkmark rows indicate controls and estimator.
The text states individual-level clustering, triangular kernel weights centred at the cutoff, speed limit fixed effects and CCT optimal bandwidth; table and figure notes repeat the clustering level.

The IV table stacks first stage, reduced form and IV panels, and reports control mean, an elasticity row, bandwidth and observations; IV coefficients are rescaled and the scaling is stated in the notes.
Controls are added as a separate column in the RD table and are included in all IV columns, with the stated purpose of improving precision.
Standard errors are clustered at the individual level in all RD and IV estimates; no explicit rationale for this level is given.
Honest confidence intervals in the sense of Armstrong and Kolesar are reported in an appendix figure to account for bias, alongside CCT robust bias-corrected intervals in the main table.

In the balance table the author counts how many of the tested covariates are significant against the number expected by chance and then relies on the summary index rather than adjusting individual tests.
observations.note: Retained after the 2026-09-09 outcome-claim sweep: the sentence records the counting rule used to read the balance table, without giving the count.

observations.statement: A footnote states that 2SLS is used for the IV ratio so that standard errors are correct rather than dividing reduced form by first stage.
Manipulation is assessed graphically: the running variable density around the cutoff is plotted with the fine size on a second axis in the same figure; no formal density test statistic is reported.
Balance appears as RD estimates on each predetermined covariate in two columns of the descriptives table (baseline and CCT), combined with a covariate-index RD plot.
The first stage (fine jump at the cutoff) is reported as Panel A of the IV table for the full sample and by income quartile, and shown graphically; no weak-IV statistic is reported.
Bandwidth sensitivity is shown in an appendix figure; the text stresses that the main bandwidth is chosen by a data-driven method to tie the author's hands.
observations.quote: Although I tie my hands by selecting the optimal estimation window

observations.statement: Placebo cutoffs are randomly reallocated to speeds where fines do not jump and the RD is re-run; results are in an appendix figure.
Non-traffic crime is used as a placebo-type outcome, with the reasoning that the sample rarely commits such crimes; results are in the appendix.

A dedicated robustness subsection covers a second-order polynomial, CCT robust estimation, honest CIs, bandwidth variation, controls and placebo cutoffs, with nearly all evidence placed in appendix tables and figures.

The RD is re-estimated with all speed limit zones, with speeding-only outcomes, with an extended follow-up horizon, and using fixed-fine cutoff variation, each referenced from a footnote to an appendix figure.

To probe generalization the estimation sample is reweighted by logit-predicted probabilities of not appearing in the speeding sample, built from all car owners in the registers; this is reported as an appendix table column.

Heterogeneity by income quartile is estimated separately per quartile at both the income-based and the fixed-fine cutoff; the fixed-fine cutoff serves as a comparison where the fine does not vary with income.
Additional splits by prior speeding history and by tertiles of municipal enforcement intensity are reported in the appendix and explicitly caveated as imprecise and possibly confounded.

Two competing frictions (adjustment costs vs information frictions) are set up ex ante with opposing predictions for ex post reactions; a stylized model section and a prediction table map findings to models.
Alternative memory-based interpretations of fade-out are discussed in a separate subsection, and two mechanical explanations are checked using the control-group time path and an appendix figure.

Effects are shown in three panels: point estimates, control-group means, and estimates relative to control means over horizons; IV effects are expressed per euro and as elasticities computed from ratios of relative changes.

A counterfactual safety-neutral fixed fine is computed from quartile IV estimates via a stated formula, expressed as a share of monthly income, with sensitivity to the imprecise bottom-quartile estimate in a footnote.
The author states that avoidance behaviour cannot be tested because camera identifiers are missing, and argues the intensive-margin design mitigates the concern.
Rare accident outcomes are flagged as limiting power; fade-out interpretation is cautioned because a stable RD estimate can shrink relative to a growing control mean.
Generalization from drivers near the cutoff to the car-owning population is addressed through reweighting; the counterfactual exercise is labelled local and holds income composition fixed.

Figures include raw density plots by speed zone and normalized pooled versions, binned outcome-by-running-variable plots, and coefficient-over-horizon plots with shaded bands; notes state clustering and refer to the sample-construction section.
Tables report standard errors in parentheses without significance stars; the descriptives table doubles as the balance table with means for the full sample and a narrow window.
Appendix figures are labelled A.x, appendix tables B.x, and theory appendices C.x; the appendix itself is only available as online supplementary material.
The introduction previews each main result in order, then gives contribution paragraphs organized by literature, and closes with a roadmap.

Order is institutions and data, descriptive bunching evidence, RD specification with validity, results, heterogeneity, additional results, robustness, then a theory section and a policy counterfactual; most checks live in the appendix.
The theoretical model is presented after the empirical results and is explicitly positioned as rationalizing them, with propositions stated in text and proofs deferred to an appendix.
A data availability statement says public data and all programs are in a Zenodo repository, confidential data cannot be shared, and the README explains how to obtain them.
Data are Finnish administrative registers (police, Statistics Finland) linked via personal identifiers, plus anonymous traffic-station data; the police data were obtained by working with the police.
No statistical software is named in the main text.
